name: USA for UNHCR: grants to UNHCR (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: USA for UNHCR's 2025 grants by region (Form 990 Schedule F, cash and goods: Sub-Saharan Africa $19.7M, Middle East and North Africa $12.1M, South Asia $8.2M, Europe $6.0M, South America $3.9M, Russia and neighbouring states $2.2M, North America $1.1M, East Asia and the Pacific $0.6M) spread over the largest UNHCR refugee operations in each region (Sudan's neighbours and Sudan, Uganda, Ethiopia, the DRC; Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, Egypt; Bangladesh, Afghanistan, Pakistan; Ukraine and Moldova; Colombia, Peru, Ecuador; Mexico; Myanmar). A judgment where no country split is published.
summary: USA for UNHCR raises money in the United States for UNHCR, the UN refugee agency: in 2025 it spent $95.5 million, of which $44.3 million went as cash grants to UNHCR's operations (most to Sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East and South Asia), $10.6 million of donated clothes, hygiene kits, software and transport passed on (the donors' resources, so credited by share rather than costed), and $8.2 million on awareness work; fundraising took $26.6 million, so each cash dollar granted costs about $1.61 of donations. The grants are valued as UNHCR's 2025 programme mix (its audited impact areas, split further by judgment): cash, relief items and shelter (excess deaths averted and goods on the site's log-income scale), health care in camps (deaths averted), registration, documents and protection services (consumption and mental-health gains), education, livelihoods, and resettlement and returns. Neither USA for UNHCR nor UNHCR counts who this money reached, so every branch rests on judged costs per person and the research on its kind of work and is discounted for missing data. It comes to about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000 (combined range 0.014-0.27: the result is mostly uncertainty), mostly because about 38% of each cash dollar pays for fundraising and management in the US and a quarter of UNHCR's for its own support costs; the biggest uncertainties are the missing-data discount, how many refugees' papers bring them rights, and how poor the people reached are.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Your dollar's share

rows.label: Share of UNHCR's spending on basic needs, shelter and water (relief)
rows.explainer: The audited impact area 2 (45% of spending) less the judged health and education shares: about {{row:rel_share}}. Cross-check: UNHCR's Global Report 2025 puts the basic needs outcome area at $689M (18%) and shelter at about $285M (7.5%), with water 3-5%.

rows.label: Share of UNHCR's spending on health and nutrition
rows.explainer: Anchor: the healthy-lives outcome area's 2025 budget was $531M (Global Appeal 2025) of $10.1 billion of needs, about 5%, and UNHCR funds health above its average because it is life-saving; the realizing-rights impact area that holds basic needs, shelter, health, education and water spent $1,708M (Table IV.3), leaving about $730M for the last three after basic needs and shelter. Judgment 7% (4-10%).

rows.label: Share of UNHCR's spending on education
rows.explainer: Anchor: the education budget was $481M in the Global Appeal 2025 (about 5% of needs) and its expenditure fell 28% in 2025 (Global Report 2025). Judgment 5% (3-8%).

rows.label: Share of UNHCR's spending on self-reliance and livelihoods
rows.explainer: Anchor: Global Report 2025 says flexible funding paid 34% ($55M) of the self-reliance, economic inclusion and livelihoods outcome area, so about $160M, 4.2% of the total. Judgment 4.2% (3-6%).

rows.label: Share of UNHCR's spending on protection (the rest)

rows.label: UNHCR's cost per person reached with cash, relief items, shelter or water
rows.explainer: Already a full cost, support included: UNHCR delivered $481M of cash itself in 2025 (A/81/5/Add.6, note 6.3) plus more through partners and $269M of relief supplies; its cash grants run from one-off winter or emergency payments of $50-150 a person to monthly help in the Middle East, and shelter kits cost more. With support costs: judgment $60 a person ($30-150). Reference class: $30 for World Vision's relief, $40 for Save the Children's emergencies.

rows.label: People reached by the relief share of the grants
Cost per person reached, with USA for UNHCR's overhead
rows.explainer: Context: what a donor pays per person reached with relief.

rows.label: Death rate among the people reached, without the response
rows.explainer: Refugees and displaced people reached with cash and relief live in camps in Sudan's neighbours, Uganda, Bangladesh and Ethiopia, and in towns of Lebanon, Jordan, Türkiye, Ukraine and Colombia. UNHCR's camp standard is a crude death rate under 0.75 per 1,000 a month (0.009 a year); new emergencies (Sudanese arrivals in Chad, eastern DRC) exceed 1 per 10,000 a day (0.037). Judgment 0.013 a person-year (0.009-0.025).

rows.label: Death rate in the same population before the crisis
rows.explainer: The site's crude death rates (UN WPP) of three of the largest refugee origins, so only excess deaths count.

rows.label: Share of the excess deaths the relief averts among the people reached
rows.explainer: Cash, relief items, shelter and water remove a small part of the extra deaths of displacement for those they reach: the Cochrane review of cash in disasters (Pega et al. 2015) found weak evidence; long-running cash programmes cut under-five deaths by about 8% (Richterman et al. 2023). Reference class: 4% for Save the Children's emergencies, 3% for the American Red Cross's relief, 0.75% for MSF's item distributions. Judgment 4% (1-10%).

rows.label: Years of the crisis the relief covers per person
rows.explainer: One-off emergency and winter payments cover a few months, monthly cash in the Middle East a year. Judgment half a year (3-12 months).

rows.label: Deaths averted per person reached (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Excess deaths over the time covered, times the share averted.

rows.label: Share of the deaths averted that are of children under five
rows.explainer: Crisis deaths are young; the family guide's range from mortality surveys. No shared age split for refugee deaths exists, and the shares move the result by a few percent.

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: The relief models' shared figure (@death_ages.crisis_share_5_14_of_over5, 20%, 10-40%): most deaths over five in crises are of adults.

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: Adult deaths in displacement split between working-age adults and older people with chronic disease; 50% as the family guide.

rows.label: Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's one value of a death, by age band, times your value of a life.

rows.label: Illness averted per person reached, in DALYs (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Diarrhoea and respiratory illness averted by water, sanitation, shelter and blankets over half a year. A moderate diarrhoeal episode weighs 0.188 for about 5 days (GBD 2019), 0.0026 DALYs: about one episode averted per person. As Save the Children's emergencies.

rows.label: Share of the relief cost that reaches people as cash or goods
rows.explainer: The rest is UNHCR's staff, transport, warehousing, partners' costs and support. Cash programmes pass 75-85% of their cost to recipients; relief items and shelter less. Judgment 60% (45-75%).

rows.label: Cash and goods delivered per person (US$)
rows.explainer: Valued as consumption, in full: the deaths and illness averted above are a small share of the people reached, so it isn't counted twice.

rows.label: US prices of 2017 per 2025 dollar
rows.explainer: Turns 2025 dollars into 2017 dollars before the 2017 PPP factor (Convention 8).

rows.label: Grants to the four regions with stand-in countries
Weight of Kenya (stand-in for Sub-Saharan Africa)
Weight of Lebanon (stand-in for the Middle East)
Weight of Bangladesh (stand-in for South Asia)
Weight of Ukraine (stand-in for Europe and its neighbours)
PPP conversion (2017 international $ per US $)
rows.explainer: The site's factors for four stand-in countries (Kenya for the African camps, Lebanon, Bangladesh, Ukraine), weighted by USA for UNHCR's grants by region.

rows.label: US prices of 2017 per 2024 dollar
rows.explainer: Puts the 2024 national-accounts figures into 2017 prices, the PPP factors' base.

rows.label: Refugees' consumption as a share of their host country's survey mean
rows.explainer: Refugees consume well below their hosts: most Syrian refugees in Lebanon live below the survival minimum expenditure basket (UNHCR, UNICEF and WFP's yearly vulnerability assessment), refugees in Kenya's and Uganda's camps live mostly on aid rations, Rohingya in Cox's Bazar below Bangladesh's poor; Ukrainians displaced in Ukraine nearer the national mean. Judgment 45% (25-75%).

rows.label: Baseline consumption, Kenya stand-in (2017 PPP $)
rows.explainer: The World Bank's household-survey mean for Kenya (2021 PPP $ a day) a year, grown to 2024, into 2024 US$ by the price level, then into the 2017 PPP base like the relief.

rows.label: Baseline consumption, Lebanon stand-in (2017 PPP $)
rows.explainer: National-accounts consumption on the survey scale (the shared world-median ratio).

rows.label: Baseline consumption, Bangladesh stand-in (2017 PPP $)
rows.explainer: National-accounts consumption on the survey scale (the shared world-median ratio).

rows.label: Baseline consumption, Ukraine stand-in (2017 PPP $)
rows.explainer: National-accounts consumption on the survey scale (the shared world-median ratio).

rows.label: Consumption per person per year of the people reached (2017 PPP $)
rows.formula: w_kenya * baseline_kenya + w_lebanon * baseline_lebanon + w_bangladesh * baseline_bangladesh + w_ukraine * baseline_ukraine
rows.explainer: The stand-in countries' refugee baselines, weighted by the grants' regions (normalization.md 2.14: survey consumption of the people served).

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person
rows.formula: years_exposed * ln(1 + value_delivered_per_person * price_2017_per_2025 * ppp_factor / (baseline_consumption * years_exposed))
rows.explainer: The site's rule for cash and goods used up within a year: the months covered × ln(1 + the transfer ÷ the consumption of those months).

rows.label: UNHCR's cost per person-year of health and nutrition care (delivery, before support costs)
rows.explainer: UNHCR funds primary health care, nutrition treatment, reproductive health and referrals in camps and settlements, mostly through partners and national health systems; humanitarian primary care costs about $10-30 a person-year. Judgment $15 ($6-40).

rows.label: Person-years of health care funded
Death rate of the refugees covered by the care
rows.explainer: UNHCR's health information system reports crude death rates in its camps of around 0.2-0.5 per 1,000 a month (0.003-0.006 a year) in stable camps and more in new emergencies; the population is young. Judgment 0.006 a person-year (0.004-0.012).

rows.label: Share of the covered refugees' deaths the health and nutrition care averts
rows.explainer: Without care, child deaths from pneumonia, diarrhoea, malaria, measles and malnutrition and maternal deaths would be far higher: community case management and nutrition treatment each cut child deaths by a fifth to a half for those reached (Lassi & Bhutta 2015; cohort studies of acute malnutrition treatment). Averaged over everyone covered: judgment 12% (4-25%).

rows.label: Deaths averted per person-year of care
Illness averted, as a share of the deaths' value
rows.explainer: Illness, malnutrition and stunting averted, births attended, HIV and chronic disease treated; GiveWell's supplementary illness shares for child-health programmes run 5-20%, and adult care adds more. Judgment 15% (0-40%).

rows.label: UNHCR's cost per refugee child supported in school for a year (delivery, before support costs)
rows.explainer: UNHCR mostly pays to include refugee children in national schools (teachers' pay, classrooms, fees, catch-up classes) and some university scholarships (DAFI, a few thousand dollars each). Judgment $150 a child ($60-300). Reference class: $130 for Save the Children's education in crises.

rows.label: Refugee children supported
Learning gained per child supported (standard deviations)
rows.explainer: The median effect on learning of randomised evaluations of education programmes in low- and middle-income countries, 0.10 SD (Evans & Yuan 2022); 0.03 for school-management programmes, 0.2 for well-run remedial teaching. For a child kept in school who would otherwise be out of it, more. As Save the Children's education branch.

rows.label: Adult earnings gain per SD of skill still there in adult life
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for low- and middle-income countries (@education.earnings_gain_per_sd_adult_skills_lmic: 20%, 10% to 30%), from the Center for Global Development's review of the studies linking adults' reading and maths to their earnings, per SD of skill still there in adult life.

rows.label: Share of the learning gain that lasts into adult work
rows.explainer: The site's one figure (@education.test_gain_persistence_to_adulthood: 40%, 20% to 70%): test-score gains fade, a fifth to a half of a year's learning carrying into the next grade in Pakistan's schools (Andrabi and others 2011).

rows.label: Years until the children start work
rows.explainer: Refugee pupils supported are mostly in primary school (aged 6-13), some in secondary or university: work starts in 6 years for the oldest, 15 for the youngest. Judgment 10 years (6-15).

rows.label: Working years the gain lasts
rows.explainer: The shared figure.

rows.label: People who share an earner's gain
rows.explainer: The shared figure, as direct-health's later-income rows.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per child, discounted
rows.formula: ln(1 + edu_learning_gain_sd * edu_earnings_per_sd * edu_persistence) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, working_years) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ (0 - edu_years_until_work) * resource_sharing_multiplier
rows.explainer: ln(1 + learning gain × earnings per SD × persistence) for each working year, discounted, after the wait to adult work, shared with the household.

rows.label: UNHCR's cost per refugee household in livelihood support (delivery, before support costs)
rows.explainer: Vocational training, start-up grants, graduation programmes with partners and advocacy for the right to work; graduation packages cost $500-1,500 a household, training and small grants less. Judgment $250 ($100-600). Reference class: $200 for Save the Children's livelihoods.

rows.label: Refugee households supported
People per household
rows.explainer: The site's household sizes for three of the largest refugee-hosting countries where UNHCR runs livelihood work (Uganda, Bangladesh, Kenya).

rows.label: Consumption gain per household member
rows.explainer: Graduation programmes for refugees and the poorest raise consumption about 5-10% for years (Banerjee et al. 2015); cheaper training and grants much less, and refugees' work is often restricted by law. Judgment 4% (1-10%).

rows.label: Years a refugee household's livelihood gain lasts
rows.explainer: Graduation trials still find consumption gains three years on (Banerjee et al. 2015), but UNHCR's cheaper training and grants fade sooner, and refugees' moves and work restrictions cut gains short. Judgment 2.5 years, from 1 (training alone, fading in a year) to 5 (a lasting business or job).

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person, over the years it lasts
rows.explainer: As cash-income's recurring-gain recipe.

rows.label: Share of protection spending on services to survivors and children (gender-based violence, child protection, psychosocial care)
rows.explainer: The rest is registration and documentation, refugee status determination, legal aid, protection monitoring and advocacy with governments. In UNHCR's results framework the gender-based violence and child protection outcome areas are each a few percent of the budget. Judgment 30% (15-45%).

rows.label: Cost per person given protection services (delivery, before support costs)
rows.explainer: Case management for survivors of violence and unaccompanied children costs hundreds of dollars a case; group psychosocial support and safe spaces tens. Judgment $80 ($30-200). Reference class: $60 for Save the Children's child protection.

rows.label: People given protection services
Share of people in conflict-affected populations with a mental disorder
rows.explainer: The shared WHO prevalence in conflict-affected populations (@humanitarian_response.conflict_mental_disorder_prevalence, 22.1%, 18.8-25.7%). Survivors of violence and separated children are at higher risk than the average refugee; people without a disorder are counted at nothing here.

rows.label: Improvement in mental health for those with a disorder (SD)
rows.explainer: Meta-analyses of psychosocial interventions in humanitarian settings find small to moderate falls in post-traumatic stress symptoms (Purgato et al. 2018); case management and survivors' care do somewhat more for the few who get them. As Save the Children's protection branch.

rows.label: Years the improvement lasts (linear fade)
rows.explainer: Trials measure a few months after the sessions. As Save the Children's protection branch.

rows.label: WELLBYs per person given services
rows.explainer: Share with a disorder × improvement × years ÷ 2 (linear fade) × the shared WELLBYs per SD-year.

rows.label: Cost per refugee registered, documented or given legal help (delivery, before support costs)
rows.explainer: UNHCR's biometric registration and documents cost a few dollars a record, refugee status determination and legal aid tens to hundreds per case, and monitoring and advocacy reach whole populations. Judgment $25 a person ($10-80).

rows.label: Refugees registered, documented or given legal help
Share of people documented whose papers bring legal work or host services they wouldn't otherwise get
rows.explainer: Most refugees UNHCR documents in a year are already registered (renewals, verification) or in hosts that grant no rights on UNHCR papers. Anchors: new asylum claims and recognitions are a few million a year against about 40 million refugees and asylum-seekers under UNHCR's care (UNHCR, Global Trends: Forced Displacement in 2024), so under a tenth of those documented are new; about half of refugees live in hosts whose law gives some right to work, though few use it in practice (Center for Global Development, Refugees International and Asylum Access, Global Refugee Work Rights Report 2022); and only part of a regularisation's gain follows papers that bring services without a work permit. About 8% new × 50% in such hosts × half the gain: judgment 2% (0.5-8%).

rows.label: Consumption gain from gaining legal status (regularisation)

source.title: Ibáñez, Moya, Ortega, Rozo & Urbina (2024), Life out of the Shadows: The Impacts of Regularization Programs on the Lives of Forced Migrants
source.quote: we find the program induced improvements of 48% and 22% in consumption per capita and labor income, respectively

rows.explainer: Colombia's Permiso Especial de Permanencia for Venezuelan migrants, a regression-discontinuity estimate; the range from the earlier drafts' 18% to the 2022 working paper's 60%. A full residence and work permit, more than most papers bring.

rows.label: Consumption gain per person documented
rows.explainer: The share whose papers bring rights times the regularisation effect: about 1% at the best guesses, for a few years.

rows.label: Years the gain lasts
rows.explainer: The shared figure for how long a document or legal status helps (@humanitarian_response.legal_aid_years, 3 years, 1-6): papers and status last years, but displaced people move on and rights are often withdrawn.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person documented
rows.explainer: As cash-income's recurring-gain recipe.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person documented (refoulement, detention, violence)
rows.explainer: Protection from forced return to persecution and from arbitrary detention averts some killings; few refugees face that risk in a year and the counterfactual is unmeasured. Judgment 1 in 10,000 people (0-5 in 10,000).

rows.label: Share of solutions spending on resettlement and complementary pathways
rows.explainer: UNHCR identifies, interviews and refers refugees to resettlement states; departures fell in 2025 when the US suspended its programme. The rest is voluntary repatriation (return cash grants, notably to Syria and Afghanistan) and local integration. Judgment 15% (8-25%).

rows.label: Refugees resettled with UNHCR's help in 2025

source.title: UNHCR, Financial report and audited financial statements for the year ended 31 December 2025 and report of the Board of Auditors (A/81/5/Add.6)

rows.explainer: UNHCR's count of resettlement departures (the last figure is 2025), down from 116,420 in 2024 when the US suspended its programme.

rows.label: UNHCR's full cost per refugee resettled
rows.explainer: UNHCR's resettlement spending (its solutions spending × the resettlement share) over its 2025 departures: about {{row:sol_cost_per_departure}}, support costs included.

rows.label: Refugees resettled with the grants
Resettled refugees' consumption over the lowest US quintile's
rows.explainer: Resettled refugees earn far below natives at first and catch up over a decade (most departures went to the US, Canada, Europe and Australia); the lowest US quintile's spending is the anchor. Judgment 1 (0.6-1.5).

rows.label: Consumption per person after resettlement (2017 US$, PPP 1)
rows.explainer: The site's US consumer expenditure per person (BLS, 2024) at the lowest quintile's share, in 2017 dollars (the PPP base, a US dollar being one international dollar): about $11,400.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person resettled, discounted
rows.explainer: The log gain from the refugee's consumption to the resettled one, each year for the shared working years, discounted.

rows.label: UNHCR's cost per refugee helped home or to integrate locally (delivery, before support costs)
rows.explainer: Return cash grants are $100-400 a person (Afghanistan, Syria, Burundi) with transport and reintegration help; local integration (documents, land, naturalisation) varies. Judgment $250 ($120-600), the delivery cost; the full cost adds UNHCR's support markup.

rows.label: Refugees helped home or to integrate locally
ln(consumption) gain per person helped home
rows.formula: years_exposed * ln(1 + sol_return_cost_per_person * rel_goods_value_share * price_2017_per_2025 * ppp_factor / (baseline_consumption * years_exposed))
rows.explainer: The cash and goods given, valued as relief is (the same share reaching people, PPP, baseline and months covered).

rows.label: Share of gifts in kind that are clothes and hygiene kits for refugees
rows.explainer: Schedule F lists 'new clothes for refugees', hygiene kits, transport and 'IT goods and licenses' by region; Schedule M records $6.5M of clothing and household goods of $10.7M of goods received. Judgment 60% (40-80%).

rows.label: Recorded value of donated goods per person who gets them
rows.explainer: Our judgment, $30 ($10-80): a hygiene kit or a few items of new clothing per person. Reference class: UNFPA puts a dignity kit (pads, soap, underwear, a torch, a comb, toothbrush and toothpaste) at US$15 for donors (https://www.unfpa.org/donate/DignityKits) and lists a customised kit in its procurement catalogue at a price of up to US$30 (https://globalsupply.unfpa.org/products/customized-dignity-kit-for-price-less-than-30-usd-1001916.html); new clothing at the donors' fair market value is dearer per item, so a person given clothes and a kit sits at the top.

rows.label: Donated clothes given to US refugee groups in 2025

source.title: USA for UNHCR (United States Association for UNHCR), Form 990 for calendar 2025 (filed August 2026; Part XII: financial statements audited), IRS e-file XML

rows.explainer: Schedule I: $628,085 to Good360 and $143,884 to the International Rescue Committee, for refugees in the US; valued at US consumption below.

rows.label: Refugees in the US who get donated clothes
Refugees abroad who get donated goods
ln(consumption) gain per refugee in the US given clothes
rows.explainer: Clothes given in the US at the shared US figures for donated goods (US value per recorded dollar × goods in kind against cash), against the lowest US quintile's spending per person (BLS 2024); both in current dollars.

rows.label: Value to refugees as a share of the donors' recorded value
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 45% (25-75%), for goods given abroad. Reference class: the site's shared figures put donated goods given in the US at about 60% of their recorded value (@united_states.donated_goods_value_vs_recorded 0.85 × @aid_value.inkind_goods_vs_cash 0.7, Wydick et al. 2018 on donated goods); abroad the same clothing and hygiene items cost less in local markets than their US fair market value, though traded goods' prices fall far less than the overall price level, so about three quarters of that. Refugees in the US are valued at the shared US figures (gik_us_ln_gain_per_person).

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per refugee given goods
rows.formula: ln(1 + gik_value_per_person * gik_inkind_equivalence * price_2017_per_2025 * ppp_factor / baseline_consumption)
rows.explainer: At relief's PPP factor and baseline.

rows.label: Value of donated IT and transport as a share of the same in cash to UNHCR
rows.explainer: Software licences and freight replace things UNHCR would partly have bought; donors' list prices overstate what UNHCR would have paid. Judgment 50% (20-90%).

rows.label: Extra money for UNHCR per dollar of awareness work
rows.explainer: Events, refugee stories and campaigns build the supporter base that later gives (beyond what the fundraising line already pays for) and press US officials on refugee funding, which fell sharply in 2025 regardless. No measurement exists. Judgment $0.30 (0-1.50). Reference class: $0.50 of aid kept per dollar in World Vision's advocacy.

rows.label: rel: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: 0.8 (0.6-1): the value is mostly cash and goods at cost, which needs no effect study; the deaths averted rest on weak evidence.

rows.label: rel: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 70% (45-90%): UNHCR was 36% funded in 2025 and cut cash and relief by 31%; the people reached would rarely have been helped by others, though WFP, NGOs and hosts cover some of the same people.

rows.label: rel: UNHCR's (or USA for UNHCR's) share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: 85% (70-100%): partners and host governments add their own staff and supplies to UNHCR's distributions.

rows.label: hlt: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: 0.6 (0.3-0.9): the treatments' effects are well measured, but how much funding care for refugees adds to their survival isn't measured here.

rows.label: hlt: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 70% (50-90%): in some hosts refugees use national clinics that would treat them anyway; in camps UNHCR's partners are often the only care.

rows.label: hlt: UNHCR's (or USA for UNHCR's) share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: 60% (40-85%): host health systems, UNICEF's therapeutic food and vaccines and partners' own funds are part of the care. Reference class: 50% for Save the Children's health.

rows.label: edu: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: 0.6 (0.3-1): programmes at scale do less than the trials' median (Evans & Yuan 2022); schooling in displacement is often interrupted. As Save the Children's education.

rows.label: edu: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 85% (60-100%): few refugee children would get another place; national schools take some anyway.

rows.label: edu: UNHCR's (or USA for UNHCR's) share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: 60% (40-85%): national schools and teachers paid by hosts carry much of the cost of the children UNHCR supports.

rows.label: liv: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: 0.75 (0.4-1): the trials' gains are small and imprecise. As Save the Children's livelihoods.

rows.label: liv: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 90% (70-100%): the trials' effects are against control groups who had their other options; 70% where other agencies and the World Bank's programmes run livelihood work for the same refugees (Uganda, Jordan), 100% where none does.

rows.label: liv: UNHCR's (or USA for UNHCR's) share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: 80% (60-100%): partners, the World Bank's refugee windows and refugees' own savings and labour.

rows.label: pro: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: 0.6 (0.3-0.9): the psychosocial trials' effects are small and uncertain, and the gains from documents are judged.

rows.label: pro: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 85% (60-100%): UNHCR holds the mandate for refugee registration and protection in most hosts; few others do this work.

rows.label: pro: UNHCR's (or USA for UNHCR's) share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: 70% (50-90%): host governments' asylum systems, courts and social services, and partners' staff.

rows.label: sol: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: 0.7 (0.4-1): the gain from resettlement is large and well documented in the income data; the value of return grants is the cash at cost.

rows.label: sol: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 30% (10-60%): resettlement states set the number of places; UNHCR's referral decides more who goes than how many, though without it fewer places would be filled. Returnees would mostly have gone home anyway; the grants ease the return.

rows.label: sol: UNHCR's (or USA for UNHCR's) share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: 20% (8-40%), Convention 2: resettlement states pay for travel, reception and years of support, far more than UNHCR's referral; returns use the origin state's and partners' help.

rows.label: gik: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: 0.95 (0.85-1): the goods at a judged share of their recorded value need no effect study; valuations may not match what was given.

rows.label: gik: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 75% (50-95%): some goods would have reached the same people through other charities or markets. As World Vision's gifts in kind.

rows.label: gik: USA for UNHCR's share of the resources behind the gifts
rows.formula: gik_cash_spend * overhead_ratio / (gik_cash_spend * overhead_ratio + gik_goods_granted * (gik_goods_share * gik_inkind_equivalence + (1 - gik_goods_share) * gik_services_vs_cash))
rows.explainer: Convention 2: USA for UNHCR's own cash for the programme (with overhead) over that cash plus the donated goods at their value to the recipients (the clothes and kits at the in-kind share, the software and transport at their share of cash), the donors' resources. About 6%.

rows.label: Share of the resources behind the outcome (outcome-weighted average)
rows.formula: (rel_dalys_unadjusted * rel_attribution_share + hlt_dalys_unadjusted * hlt_attribution_share + edu_dalys_unadjusted * edu_attribution_share + liv_dalys_unadjusted * liv_attribution_share + pro_dalys_unadjusted * pro_attribution_share + sol_dalys_unadjusted * sol_attribution_share + gik_dalys_unadjusted * gik_attribution_share + aw_dalys_unadjusted) / (rel_dalys_unadjusted + hlt_dalys_unadjusted + edu_dalys_unadjusted + liv_dalys_unadjusted + pro_dalys_unadjusted + sol_dalys_unadjusted + gik_dalys_unadjusted + aw_dalys_unadjusted)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own share in its own adjustments. Awareness has none (1).

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: every branch applies its own share in its own adjustments.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment (every branch)
rows.explainer: UNHCR works through partners in insecure places; the Board of Auditors found weaknesses in partner monitoring and cash reconciliations in 2025 (A/81/5/Add.6), and some aid is lost or diverted. Reference class: 85% for Save the Children's and MSF's relief.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: UNHCR's 2025 needs were 64% unfunded (A/81/5/Add.6, para 35), so another donor rarely fills the gap a grant leaves; earmarked grants may shift UNHCR's flexible money elsewhere within the same mix. 1 (0.85-1.1).

rows.label: Years from gift to grant
rows.explainer: USA for UNHCR's liabilities at the end of 2025 (mostly sums due to UNHCR and deferred gifts in kind) were $21.6M against $55M of grants a year (990 Part X), about 0.4 years at most; cash is wired through the year. Judgment 0.2 years (0.1-0.4).

rows.label: Years from grant to help
rows.explainer: UNHCR spends within its budget year (carry-over $101M of $3.8 billion in 2025, Table IV.3); school, livelihood and resettlement help comes later in the year. Judgment 0.2 years (0.05-0.5).

rows.label: Discount for the wait
rows.explainer: The waits at the shared discount rate.

rows.label: rel: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin: UNHCR publishes no count of people reached by this grant money; reach is spending over a judged cost, and the deaths averted rest on the research on cash and relief in crises. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: hlt: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin: No count of refugees covered by this money; the deaths averted are judged from trials of the treatments, not of this care. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: edu: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin: No count of children for this money and no controlled evaluation; the effect is the median of other programmes. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: liv: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin: No count of households for this money; the effect comes from trials of other programmes. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: pro: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin: No count of people served by this money and no controlled evaluation; the effects are judged from trials and studies of other work. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: sol: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin: No count of people resettled or returned with this money; reach is spending over judged costs. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: gik: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin: No count of refugees who got the goods; reach and value are judgments. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: aw: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin: No outcome data; the money brought in is a judgment. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Side effect: spending in host communities
rows.explainer: Cash and wages spent by refugees and UNHCR raise host traders' sales and wages (Taylor et al. 2016 find each dollar of cash to Congolese refugees in Rwanda raised local income by more than a dollar). +3% (0 to +8%) of the result.

rows.label: Side effect: prices, tensions and dependency
rows.explainer: In-kind aid can depress local prices; aid to refugees alone can raise tensions with poor hosts, and long camp stays keep refugees from work. -2% (-6% to 0).
